title: Surrey Warns of Fireworks Fines Up to $50,000 Ahead of Halloween and Diwali
excerpt: The B.C. city requires federal certification and a fire service permit for any fireworks, with bylaw officers and police patrolling on October 31 and November 8.
body:
• Surrey, B.C. prohibits the sale, purchase and use of fireworks without both federal certification and a Surrey Fire Service permit; possession by anyone under 18 is banned.
  • Fines run from $400 to $50,000 per offence, and each day an offence occurs counts as a separate violation.
  • Bylaw officers and police will patrol high-activity areas leading up to Halloween on October 31 and on Diwali, November 8.
  • Residents who see illegal fireworks should call Surrey Bylaws at 604-591-4370 — and reserve 911 for emergencies only.

The City of Surrey is warning residents that fireworks are prohibited across the city without proper certification and permits, as Halloween and Diwali approach — the two dates when illegal displays peak in the Metro Vancouver city, home to one of Canada's largest South Asian communities. In an October 6 notice, the city said unauthorised fireworks can lead to injuries, fires and distress for vulnerable residents and animals, a warning CBC reported as residents prepared for both celebrations.

The rules, and what breaking them costs

Under Surrey's Fireworks Regulation Bylaw No. 4200, selling, buying or using fireworks requires two things together: federal certification and a valid permit from the Surrey Fire Service. Possession by anyone under 18 is prohibited outright. The penalties were raised sharply in October 2024, when council lifted the minimum fine from $100 to $400 and the maximum from $5,000 to $50,000, according to the city's council release. Each day an offence occurs is a separate violation, and both police and bylaw officers can issue fines.

"The illegal use of fireworks poses severe risks, including potential injuries, property damage, and distress to animals."

— Brenda Locke, Mayor of Surrey

Enforcement on the two big nights

Leading up to Halloween on October 31 and on Diwali, November 8, bylaw officers will be deployed in high-activity areas across Surrey, working with police, the city said in its 2026 enforcement notice. Officers will respond to reports, gather evidence, issue tickets and engage police as needed. The city says the same strategy last year produced more than 1,150 site visits and over 130 tickets. Reports from residents help officers identify hotspots: Surrey Bylaws takes calls at 604-591-4370, while 911 is for emergencies only.

Why Surrey tightened the law

Council raised the fines after a surge in complaints in the weeks before Halloween and Diwali, Mayor Brenda Locke said when the changes passed. Joey Jatinder Singh Brar, the city's general manager of corporate services, said the higher penalties give bylaw officers and police better tools to manage firework risks, and reminded residents that only those with the right permits should use fireworks. Surrey is not alone in the region: neighbouring Fraser Valley cities including Abbotsford, Chilliwack and Hope also prohibit consumer fireworks, with Abbotsford warning of fines of up to $50,000 and confiscation.

What Surrey families should do instead

For Diwali, the practical options are permitted professional displays, community events and the city's own celebrations — not backyard fireworks, which are illegal in Surrey even on the festival day itself without the federal certification and fire service permit that few households hold. Pet owners are advised to keep animals indoors on both nights, and anyone planning a celebration near the October 31 and November 8 enforcement window should expect officers in high-activity neighbourhoods. The city closes its notice on a civic note: Surrey is proud of its diverse community and encourages safe, respectful celebrations.
